title: Abraham believed (Romans 4)
hookLine: Abraham trusted God and it was counted as righteousness

lines: AN OLD MAN UNDER THE STARS.
cards: An old man stands outside his tent at night. He's well past seventy-five. His wife Sarah is old too, long past childbearing.
They have no children, and by every sensible measure never will. And God takes him outside and says: look up, count the stars if you can. So shall your descendants be.

Centuries later, in the middle of his big argument about grace, Paul needs one example everyone in Rome respects, Jew and Gentile alike. He doesn't pick a king or a prophet. He goes back to that old man under the stars.

teach.b: Paul quotes Genesis, in the King James Bible: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness." Believed: the Greek verb shares a root with pistis, faith, and means trust more than opinion.
Abraham didn't agree to a list of ideas; he leaned his whole weight on a promise.
Counted is an accountant's word in Greek: credited, entered in the ledger as being in the right with God. Timing matters too.

teach.h: BEFORE THE SIGN, FATHER OF ALL.
teach.b: In Genesis, this verse comes before Abraham is circumcised, before the covenant sign. So, Paul says, Abraham is the father of everyone who trusts like this: his own people, and the nations too.
Abraham looked honestly at his own body, as good as dead at about a hundred, and at Sarah's, and still trusted.
Genesis is honest too: Abraham and Sarah both laugh at the promise at different moments, and they try a plan of their own along the way. Faith here is not the absence of doubt. It's trusting anyway.
Christians read this chapter alongside the letter of James, which also points to Abraham and says faith without works is dead. How the two fit has been argued over, sharply at the Reformation.
Many Protestants today hear them as two sides of one coin; Catholic and Orthodox teaching stresses that faith and works belong together. Jews and Muslims also honor Abraham as a father of faith.
After a week of big words, grace, sin, but now, it comes down to one old man, looking up, trusting.

how: Christians often point to Abraham as the model of faith, and many pray by naming a specific worry and entrusting it to God, sometimes with the words of a psalm.

o: believing something without any evidence at all
trust that leans its whole weight on a promise
agreeing to a list of ideas about God, on paper

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: so father of all who trust

s: in Genesis, Abraham never doubted or laughed at the promise
Genesis tells of Abraham and Sarah both laughing, and of a plan of their own. faith here is trusting anyway.
the Greek word for counted comes from keeping accounts
Abraham's trust was credited, entered in the ledger, as righteousness.
for Paul, faith means agreeing to a list of ideas
pistis means trust: leaning your whole weight on a promise.

games.q: you're old, with no children, and God says your descendants will be like the stars. you look at your own aging body. what do you do?
o: decide the promise must be a figure of speech.
look honestly at your body, and trust anyway.
wait until there's proof before trusting.
games.why: Paul says Abraham considered his body as good as dead, and still "against hope believed in hope."

practice: Think of one thing you're gripping tightly right now, a test result, a child far away, money, a decision you keep replaying, and hold it in your mind like something in your fist.
Look at it honestly, the way Abraham looked at his own old body, then slowly open your hand.
If you pray, hand that one thing to God and leave it there; if you don't, simply loosen your grip for two minutes and notice what happens in your chest.

wordCard.voice: Faith. Pistis in Greek: trust, leaning your weight on a promise. Abraham's was counted to him as righteousness.

orig.note: Greek: faith, trust, faithfulness. the same word can mean trusting and being trustworthy.

carryVoice: Your line: counted as right. Trust, not proof, went into Abraham's ledger. See you tomorrow.

Who against hope believed in hope
